name: John Stuart Mill
role: British philosopher, economist and Liberal MP (1806–1873)
summary: Mill was a classical-liberal utilitarian who defended individual liberty limited only by harm to others, representative government with proportional representation, and equal rights for women. In political economy he favoured laisser-faire as a general rule with wide exceptions, taxation of unearned wealth, trade unions and peasant property, and in later life looked to worker co-operatives and open experiments in socialism while rejecting central planning. He also held that benevolent despotism could be legitimate over peoples he deemed barbarians.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In Principles Book II ch. XII he examined a legal minimum wage and argued that wages fixed above the market rate leave some workers jobless unless work or wages are guaranteed to all who apply; he preferred restraint of population and workers' own combination.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Wrote that laisser-faire should be the general practice and every departure from it, unless required by some great good, is a certain evil; but he also listed large exceptions (monopolies, education, poor relief, public works).

public-ownership.rationale: Held that road, canal and railway monopolies should be reserved in reversion to the state or have their charges fixed by it, and that water and gas should be provided by municipal authorities paid by a local rate; allowed the state to own railways while companies operate them.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Mixed: rejected a graduated income tax as a penalty on industry and saving, yet called graduated legacy and inheritance duties just, and wanted unearned fortunes and land-rent increases limited or specially taxed.

unions-good.rationale: Wrote it is a great error to condemn trade unions or strikes per se and that associations of labourers are the necessary instrumentality of a free labour market; also cautioned about what strikes can achieve.

property-fundamental.rationale: Treated private property as justified by utility and subject to reform ('the principle of private property has never yet had a fair trial'); said landed property has no special sacredness and that the right of inheritance does not follow from it.
